#### Why "when" is a processing-time decision about an event-time question

A window is useless until something decides to emit it. That decision is a **trigger**, and triggers come in kinds that differ in what they are reacting to.

**A processing-time trigger fires on the clock** — every 60s, say. Following window [12:00, 12:02), it emits 8, then 15, then 15, then 15: whatever had arrived. It first reaches the right answer, 19, at 12:05:00 — and it cannot tell that firing apart from the ones before it.

**A watermark is a completeness signal:** "no event with an event time earlier than *t* will arrive." That lets a trigger make a different kind of claim — fire when the watermark passes 12:02, because the window is *done*. It fires exactly once, after event id 4 at 12:04:06, emitting **15** from ids 0, 1, 2.

15, not 19: id 7 has not arrived. **The claim of completeness and the error are the same event** — the watermark was the pipeline's best estimate and it was wrong.

**So a real pipeline wants three triggers on one window,** not a choice between them: **early** (speculative, before the watermark — 8, 15, 15), **on-time** (at the watermark — 15), and **late** (once per straggler — 19 at 12:04:40). They serve three different consumers and all three fire.

**Allowed lateness** bounds the waiting: it is how long window state is kept after the watermark passes, which is garbage collection for that state. And it has an exact threshold here. When id 7 arrives, the watermark stands at 12:03:20 (200s); state survives while the watermark is below 12:02 + allowed, so **allowed lateness must be at least 81s** for the correction to land. At 80s the state is already gone and 15 stands forever.

Note that 81s is *not* id 7's 230s of skew, which is the number a reader would guess. It comes from how far the watermark had advanced — it jumped from 12:01:10 to 12:03:05 in a single event. **The knob is calibrated against the watermark, not against the data.**

#### When to use each trigger, and what allowed lateness costs

**Use a processing-time trigger when a consumer needs a number on a schedule** and can tolerate it being provisional — a live dashboard, a progress bar. It never stalls, which is its real virtue: a watermark that stops advancing stops your output, and a clock does not.

**Use the watermark trigger when the result is meant to be an answer** rather than a status — a report, an hourly figure, anything someone will quote. It fires once per window with a meaningful claim attached.

**Use late triggers whenever correctness outranks simplicity,** and accept that your published numbers will move.

**Set allowed lateness from your skew tail, then price the memory.** It keeps window state alive, so the bill is (open windows × state per window). With 4 windows that is nothing; with a million open session windows it is the dominant cost of the pipeline.

**What this does not settle:** "when" produced 5 separate published values for ONE window, and nothing here says what a consumer should do with the second one. If a sink stored 15 and then receives 19, does it add or replace? That question is "how", and until it is answered the pipeline's correctness is undefined — not merely unoptimised.

#### Visual walkthrough — a clock trigger, a watermark trigger, and one threshold

The animation loops through all 4 steps. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch02-when/ch02-when.svg" alt="Visual walkthrough — a clock trigger, a watermark trigger, and one threshold, 4 animated steps" width="1040">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — a trigger is the thing that says "emit now"</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch02-when/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: a trigger is the thing that says &quot;emit now&quot;" width="1040">

A processing-time trigger is the simplest possible "when": fire every 60s. It is never blocked and never wrong about its own rule — and it emits 8, then 15, then 15. The right answer appears at 12:05:00, indistinguishable from the firings before it.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — a watermark lets a trigger say "the window is COMPLETE"</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch02-when/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: a watermark lets a trigger say &quot;the window is COMPLETE&quot;" width="1040">

This trigger waits for a reason rather than a clock: fire when the watermark passes 12:02. It fires exactly once, at 12:04:06, and emits 15. Compare that with the previous step: fewer firings, a meaningful claim attached to each — and still 15 rather than 19, because the watermark was wrong about completeness.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — so a pipeline wants THREE triggers, not one</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch02-when/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: so a pipeline wants THREE triggers, not one" width="1040">

The reason "when" is a question rather than a setting: these three triggers serve three different consumers, and a window fires for all of them. One window, several published results — which is exactly the situation the fourth question ("how") exists to make safe.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and allowed lateness decides whether the fix ever lands</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch02-when/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and allowed lateness decides whether the fix ever lands" width="1040">

Allowed lateness is how long a window's state is kept after the watermark passes — it bounds memory, and it decides whether a straggler can still change an answer. Here the threshold is exactly 81s: at 80s the correction is impossible and at 81s it happens. That number comes from the watermark's jump, not from the 230s of skew.

</details>
